extracted.intended_audience: aspiring fiction writers, writing students, and creative-writing instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on Dwight V. Swain's scene and sequel model for fiction: how to construct a scene (goal, conflict, disaster) and the linking sequel (reaction, dilemma, decision), with notes on pacing, plausibility, and placement of exposition. Aimed at writers structuring scenes and transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goal
rubrics_metrics.description: The focal character of the scene should have a measurable, scene-level goal, and this should (usually) be clear to the audience at the beginning of the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The audience needs to know the goal so they can measure progress and setbacks and become invested; without a clear goal readers are just 'watching stuff happen.' Make the goal scene-specific and measurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: The focal character runs into opposition on their way to the goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opposition can be obvious/direct or less obvious/indirect; it must pose opposition to achieving the goal. Conflict is the rising action of a scene and should develop and escalate to a climactic moment or turning point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disaster
rubrics_metrics.description: The conflict leads to an outcome—either the character reaches the goal or she doesn’t—and an unanticipated 'disaster' enters the story that gives the character a new problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'No, and...' or 'Yes, but...' technique; disasters should have ramifications (not necessarily earth-shattering). Nearly all scenes should end on a disaster, though some may not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequel (definition/role)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequel is a unit of transition that links two scenes; it sets forth the focal character's reaction to the scene just completed and provides motivation for the scene next to come.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sequel transitions from the disaster to a new goal and follows a natural chain of logic (reaction → dilemma → decision). It connects scenes and establishes the motivation that launches the next scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediately after the disaster the character reacts—this shows how they cope and reveals character; the reaction focuses on the character's emotions and state of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reaction may be brief or extend over long periods; sequels are often where summary is appropriate (e.g., summarizing weeks of coping rather than play-by-play). The reaction can also show effects on other characters or the state of affairs (e.g., consequences for dependents, society, or group plans). Use this phase to render emotional truth and character detail. Example (from the page): Chihiro's terror and crying after passing into the spirit world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dilemma
rubrics_metrics.description: The character considers what to do next and weighs different options—often none of the choices are promising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dilemma is more logical than reaction: the character assesses stakes (what they have to lose/gain) and feasibility of options. Include obstacles to quitting (stakes) so plot continues. This phase may include seeking advice or doing research and lets readers evaluate what they might do in the same situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision
rubrics_metrics.description: The character comes to a decision—either by logical reasoning or via a revelation/epiphany—and this decision creates a new goal that leads into the next scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New information or insight can precipitate the decision. The decision must be believable given the prior reaction and dilemma; even seemingly odd choices should feel earned by the character's emotional and logical process. Example (from the page): Chihiro eats the berry and accepts Haku's direction to get a job at the bathhouse (new goal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sequel length to control pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequels help control pacing: in fast-paced sequences sequels are typically shorter; to slow overall pacing, make sequels longer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust sequel duration to speed up or slow down the story. The longest sequel in many stories often corresponds to the 'Dark Night of the Soul' beat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequels reinforce plausibility and motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequels help reinforce plausibility by taking time to render the emotions and logic that lead to the next goal (motivation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stronger or longer sequels generally increase plausibility—within reason—because they show believable emotional/logical progression to the character's next choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequels can be brief or forced decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequel may be extremely brief if the character is forced to make a quick decision and lacks time to fully react or think.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a sequel is brief, emotional reactions may be deferred and explored later. Brief sequels often accompany action-heavy, breathless sequences where the character must act immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate placement of introspection and exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages of introspection, characters recalling past incidents, and mild information dumps usually fit best in sequels rather than scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In scenes such passages risk slowing the pacing because scenes are action-focused; readers expect sequels to slow down and allow reflection or summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene vs. sequel boundary (unit-of-scene choices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some view scenes and sequels as two types of 'scene' units: a sequel may be tagged onto the end of a scene or may function as its own scene depending on time/place/length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most define a SCENE as action in a single location and continuous time—if the sequel continues without break it might remain part of the same scene; if it shifts time/place or is lengthy it may become its own scene. Whether to treat the sequel as separate depends on story needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequel mode: summary vs. real time
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequel may be mostly summary or rendered in real time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use summary when the reaction covers long spans (days, months, years) and play-by-play isn't important; use real-time rendering when immediate emotional detail or stakes demand it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid beginning a story with a sequel (caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning a story with a sequel is tricky because a sequel is reaction to something that happened off-page, which is rarely as interesting as following a character toward conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting in medias res with the setup for a scene (goal→conflict→disaster) is usually more engaging; if you start with a sequel, handle carefully to avoid weak opening momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility and rule-breaking (meta-guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Swain's order (goal, conflict, disaster; reaction, dilemma, decision) is a useful framework but not inviolable; parts can be skipped, rearranged, or overlapped depending on story needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As you learn the pattern you'll know when to break it for effect; don't become dogmatic, but use the model as a practical tool for structuring scenes and sequels.
